world.bio: I taught secondary-school chemistry for sixteen years, then left the lab and built a 200-litre steam still in my garage in Ruiru. Now I make rose water, small batches, bottled by hand. I'm obsessive about what goes in: I measure the pH, check the colour, smell every batch. I coach my son's under-14 football team on weekends.
skills_assets: Sixteen years of secondary-school chemistry teaching
A 200-litre stainless steel steam still built to my own spec in a Ruiru garage
Distillation know-how: temperature control, cut points, hydrosol quality checks
A small customer list of about forty regular buyers in Nairobi
Basic lab glassware and a pH meter

projects.name: Rose-water batches
projects.text: My still runs two days a week at most because market roses are sprayed with who-knows-what and I won't put that in rose water. I've bought roses from three different stalls in Wakulima market and every time the smell is faintly chemical. I keep a notebook of which stall, which day, what the petals felt like.

projects.name: Land title dispute
projects.text: My family land in my home county is under dispute: a cousin claims part of the plot. Court dates keep getting pushed. It's a slow, tiring thing and I don't talk about it much.

notes.text: Ran a batch this morning with the Naivasha roses from the usual stall. Smelled the first fraction and something was off, a faint chemical edge. Threw out the whole batch. 40 litres of petals, gone. I won't sell it.
Son's team lost 3-1 on Saturday. He played well, though. He asked me after the match why I'm always smelling things. I said because the nose knows. He rolled his eyes.

Rereading 'Decolonising the Mind'. Ngũgĩ writes that language carries a whole way of seeing, and I thought about how in the lab we taught chemistry in English to children who think in Kikuyu. Old thoughts.

Went to Wakulima market again. Asked a stall owner how often they spray. He laughed and said 'weekly, otherwise they die'. I bought a small bunch anyway for my wife. I can't make rose water out of it but I can put it in a vase.
Court date moved again, third time. Lawyer says November now. I told my wife I'm fine. I'm not fine, but I've decided not to carry it into the garage.
Weekly check of the still: the condenser has a small leak, a drip every few seconds. Fixed it with a new gasket. Cost 300 shillings. The relief of a small repairable problem.
Two regular customers asked if I have more stock. I have eleven bottles. Told them next month. There's a shortage of clean petals, not of demand.
Weekend: football practice, then home. I made tea, sat in the garage and watched the still cool. There's a stillness there that I can't find anywhere else.

Wrote a list of what I'd need for a proper supply: roses with a spray record, ideally. I have no idea where such a thing exists. Ended up adding 'ask Mary' (my wife's cousin who works in horticulture).

messages.text:
Grace: How was the batch?
Me: Bad. The roses were sprayed.
Grace: You're too fussy, Daniel.
Me: Fussy is why they buy from me.

Wanjiru: Do you have the 250ml bottles in stock?
Me: Eleven left. I'm waiting on clean petals.
Wanjiru: Take your time, quality matters.

Mutua: The hearing is now 12 November.
Me: Again?
Mutua: Yes. The judge is on leave.

Brian: Dad, can we practise penalties on Saturday?
Me: Yes, but you're in goal first.
Brian: Unfair.

calendar.event: Wakulima market, test two new stalls

relations.about: Teacher; supports the business but thinks I'm fussy.
Works in horticulture, may know growers.

constraints: Won't use petals from unknown spraying practices
Still capacity is two days a week at best
Small working capital, no big purchases
Time on weekends goes to football
sensitive: Money is tight when batches fail
Fear that the business is too small to matter
